meta.title: Monopoly — one game, forty spaces
meta.description: The London board as it is: forty spaces round the edge, nine between each corner. Follow two players round it — a purchase, an auction, a set completed, three turns in a cell, a hotel on Mayfair and the landing that ends the game. Pipe colour is the money: green to and from the bank, amber between players, red for the one shortcut nobody wants. Two squares open into scenes of their own.
Forty spaces, four corners, nine between each. Every game of Monopoly ever played happened on this rectangle.
meta.notes: The middle is where the box art and the two card decks live.

meta.description: The cheap side. Two brown properties nobody wants and the first station.
Pink and orange — the stretch most likely to be landed on out of jail.
Red and yellow, the middle of the board and the middle of the market.
The expensive side. Park Lane and Mayfair end more games than anything else.
GO — the only square that pays you.
meta.notes: Collect £200 every time you pass it, including the time you land on it. Not £400 for landing: that is a house rule too.
The cheapest street on the board and, with a hotel, still only £250. People buy it out of affection.
Doctor’s fee, sale of stock, second prize in a beauty contest. Two of the sixteen send you somewhere.
The other brown. Cheap to complete, cheap to develop, and hotels here cost £50 apiece.
Current rules make it a flat £200. Older sets let you choose 10% of everything you own instead, which almost nobody works out honestly.
Rent is £25 for one station, £50 for two, £100 for three, £200 for all four. Stations cannot be built on.
Light blue. Cheap to complete and directly in the firing line of anyone leaving jail.

meta.description: Chance — 16 cards, ten of which move you.
meta.notes: The most dangerous deck: three cards send you to jail or backwards, and one sends you to Mayfair.
The middle light blue. Worth more to whoever already owns the other two than it is to you.
Completes the light blues. With the set the rent doubles to £16 before a single house goes on.

meta.description: Jail, and the Just Visiting kerb outside it.
meta.notes: Two different squares sharing one corner. Visiting costs nothing; being in costs you up to three turns.

meta.description: Your token is in jail. You still collect rent, still trade, still build.
meta.notes: Being in jail late in the game is an advantage: you cannot land on anyone else’s hotels from inside it.

meta.description: One attempt per turn, three turns in all.
meta.notes: Six of the thirty-six outcomes are doubles, so each attempt succeeds one time in six. You move the number thrown and do not roll again.

meta.description: The fine. Optional on turns one and two, compulsory on turn three.
meta.notes: Paying before you roll lets you use both dice normally, including a double for an extra turn.

meta.description: One card in each deck. Play it or sell it to another player.
meta.notes: It goes to the bottom of its deck once used, so there is always exactly one of each in circulation.

meta.description: Out on the Just Visiting kerb, moving the number you threw.
meta.notes: The oranges and pinks sit six to nine squares from here, which is why they are the best sets in the game.
First of the pinks, and one of the most landed-on stretches on the board thanks to everyone leaving jail six to nine squares away.
Rent is four times your dice roll, or ten times if the same player owns Water Works too. Never a fortune, never nothing.
The pink nobody remembers until they owe £500 on it.
Completes the pinks. A pink set with three houses each is the classic mid-game trap.
The second station. Two stations is £50 a landing — the cheapest reliable income on the board.
First of the oranges, statistically the best set on the board: everyone leaving jail rolls into them.

meta.description: Community Chest — the second of three.
meta.notes: All three squares draw from the same deck, and cards go to the bottom after use.
The middle orange. Three houses here is £700 a landing for an outlay of £600.
Completes the oranges, six to nine squares out of jail — the single most profitable spot to be waiting.
No money, no cards, no penalty. Every pot of cash in the middle of a real game is a house rule.
First of the reds, and the beginning of the expensive half of the board.
Ten of the sixteen cards move your token. Drawing here can take you back to Old Kent Road.
The middle red. Unimproved it is small change; with a hotel it is £1,050.
One of the most landed-on squares in the game — a Chance card posts players here from three places on the board.
The third station. Chance cards send players to the nearest station and charge them double.
First of the yellows. Expensive to build, awkwardly placed, frequently owned by the player who then loses.
The middle yellow. Nothing distinguishes it except how often it is mortgaged.
Four times the dice, or ten times with the Electric Company. Buy it to stop someone else getting the pair.
Completes the yellows, and sits one square before Go To Jail. Many players never land on it at all.

meta.description: Go To Jail — the worst square on the board.
meta.notes: Straight to the cell, no £200, no collecting anything on the way. You are not "just visiting".
First of the greens. Greens cost £200 a house and rarely repay it before the game ends.
The middle green. A full green set with hotels is the most expensive thing to build in the game.

meta.description: Community Chest — the last of three.
meta.notes: The deck that pays you £100 for a life insurance policy and takes £150 for school fees.
Completes the greens. £1,100 to build them out to hotels; you had better collect.
The fourth station. Owning all four is £200 a landing and needs no building at all.

meta.description: Chance — the last of three, and the cruellest.
meta.notes: It sits two squares before Mayfair, and one of its cards is "Advance to Mayfair".
The quieter dark blue. Four houses here is £1,100 — and the rules make you build it before Mayfair gets a hotel.
A flat £100, and the last thing between a player and Mayfair.
The most expensive square in the game. £50 unimproved, £100 with the set, £2,000 with a hotel. Games end here.

meta.description: Mayfair as bought: a title deed and nothing on it.
meta.notes: Rent £50. Doubled to £100 the moment the same player owns Park Lane as well, with nothing built.
The first house is the best value on the board: it multiplies the rent by four for a quarter of the purchase price.
Another £200 for another £400 of rent.
Three houses is where most sets stop, because it is where the money runs out.
The worst step on the ladder: £200 spent for £300 more rent.

meta.description: £200 and the four houses, traded in. Rent £2,000.
meta.notes: A hotel replaces the houses — they go back to the bank for someone else to buy. Only twelve hotels exist.

meta.description: The rent ladder printed on the card: 50 · 200 · 600 · 1400 · 1700 · 2000.
meta.notes: Also on the card: houses cost £200 each here, and mortgaging raises £200.

meta.description: The other dark blue, built at the same rate.
meta.notes: You may never be more than one house ahead on either street of a set. Mayfair cannot reach a hotel until Park Lane has four houses.

meta.description: Pays out, collects, and never runs out — the rules say so.
meta.notes: It also auctions any property a player declines to buy, and it is where every house and hotel comes from. There are only 32 houses and 12 hotels in the box, and running out is a legal way to starve your opponents.

meta.description: Player 1. Starts on GO with £1,500 and a plan about light blues.
meta.notes: Opening cash is £1,500: two £500s, two £100s, two £50s, six £20s, five each of £10, £5 and £1.

meta.description: Player 2. Starts on GO with the same £1,500 and rather worse luck.
meta.notes: Turn order is decided by a roll before the game starts. It matters less than people think.

meta.description: Sixteen Chance cards, shuffled face down.
meta.notes: Ten of them move your token, three of those to jail or backwards. The Get Out Of Jail Free card lives in here until someone draws it.

meta.description: Sixteen Community Chest cards, shuffled face down.
meta.notes: Mostly small sums in your favour, plus a second Get Out Of Jail Free card and one trip to jail.

steps.name: Overview
steps.title: The board
steps.description: Forty spaces, four corners, two players and a bank in the middle. Nothing has happened yet.

footer.text: Pipe colour is the money: **green** to and from the bank, **amber** between players, **red** for the shortcut to jail.

steps.name: Boot rolls six
steps.title: The boot opens with a six
steps.description: Four and a two. The token crosses six pipes and stops on The Angel Islington, unowned and cheap.

steps.name: Buys the Angel
steps.title: The boot buys The Angel Islington
steps.description: Land on an unowned property and you may buy it at the printed price, there and then. £100 goes to the bank and the deed comes back.

footer.text: Boot: **£1,400** left. One third of a light blue set.

steps.name: Hat rolls four
steps.title: The top hat rolls a four
steps.description: Three and a one. Four spaces off GO is Income Tax, which is not a property and cannot be bought, avoided or negotiated.

steps.name: Income Tax
steps.title: Income Tax takes £200
steps.description: The hat pays the bank and gets nothing for it. Fourth space of the game, thirteen percent of his money gone.

annotations.text: pay(£200) — flat rate, no property acquired

footer.text: **£200** flat in the current rules. Older sets let you pay 10% of everything you own instead — which you must decide **before** you count it.

steps.name: Boot rolls three
steps.title: The boot takes Pentonville Road
steps.description: Three spaces on, past Chance and Euston Road, and the boot lands on Pentonville and buys it for £120.

footer.text: Two light blues owned, one to go — and the one to go is **Euston Road**, two spaces behind him.

steps.name: Hat rolls four
steps.title: The hat lands on Euston Road and declines
steps.description: Euston Road is £100 and useless to him — the boot owns the other two light blues. He passes on it.

steps.name: The auction
steps.title: Declining sends it to auction instead
steps.description: A property nobody buys does not stay on the shelf: the bank auctions it immediately, and anyone may bid. The boot pays £260 for a £100 street because it completes his set.

footer.text: Auctions are in the rules and almost nobody plays them. They are the fastest way sets get completed.
Set complete. Unimproved rent **doubles** at once — Pentonville £8 → £16 — before a single house goes on.

steps.name: Hat rolls nine
steps.title: The hat rolls nine into Community Chest
steps.description: Five and a four, past the whole light blue set he just handed over, and onto Community Chest.

steps.name: Draws a card
steps.title: Community Chest pays out
steps.description: Top card off the deck, read aloud, obeyed, then put to the bottom. This one is a dividend: the bank pays £50.

footer.text: Ten of the sixteen Chance cards move your token. Community Chest mostly just moves money.

steps.name: Free Parking
steps.title: The boot rolls eleven onto Free Parking
steps.description: Eleven spaces, the length of one side of the board, and he lands on the corner everyone has an opinion about.

footer.text: Free Parking pays **nothing**. No fines pot, no jackpot, no bonus — the pile of cash in the middle is a house rule, and it makes games longer.

steps.name: Hat buys Fleet St
steps.title: The hat rolls six and buys Fleet Street
steps.description: A red, £220, rent £18 while it stands alone. He needs Strand and Trafalgar Square to make it mean anything.

steps.name: Boot rolls three
steps.title: The boot lands on Fleet Street too
steps.description: Three spaces from Free Parking, past Strand and Chance, onto a street the hat bought a minute ago. Two tokens can share a square; only one of them owes anything.

steps.name: Rent: £18
steps.title: The boot pays rent — eighteen pounds
steps.description: Rent on an unimproved street with no set behind it. The owner has to ask for it before the next player rolls, or it is forfeit.

footer.text: Remember this number. **£18.** It is the same board, the same rulebook, and the same two players as the £2,000 at the end.

steps.name: Hat rolls seven
steps.title: The hat rolls a seven — the commonest roll there is
steps.description: Six ways out of thirty-six to make a seven, and every one of them lands him on Go To Jail.

steps.name: Go to jail
steps.title: Go directly to jail
steps.description: The only square that moves you against your will and pays you nothing for the journey. The token crosses the board on the red pipe.

annotations.text: goToJail() — no GO, no £200, no landings on the way

footer.text: **Do not pass GO. Do not collect £200.** Nothing on the squares between happens either.

steps.name: Three ways out
steps.title: Inside, there are exactly three ways out
steps.description: Throw a double, pay £50, or play a Get Out Of Jail Free card. You get three turns to try, and you keep collecting rent the whole time.

footer.text: Jail is not a penalty box. You still own, trade, build and charge rent from inside it — you just cannot land on anyone else’s hotels.

steps.name: Three failed tries
steps.title: Three turns, three attempts at a double
steps.description: One roll per turn. Six of the thirty-six outcomes are pairs, so each attempt fails five times in six — and all three fail more often than not.

footer.text: Failing all three is the **likelier** outcome, at 125 in 216.

steps.name: Pays the fifty
steps.title: On the third turn the £50 is compulsory
steps.description: Having thrown no double and holding no card, the hat pays the fine and moves the number he just threw. Out on the kerb, £50 lighter.

footer.text: Paying the £50 **before** rolling on turn one costs the same and buys three clean turns of movement. Most players wait, and most players are wrong.

steps.name: Out and moving
steps.title: The hat comes out onto Vine Street
steps.description: Nine spaces from the jail corner, which is exactly why the oranges and pinks are the most valuable ground in the game.

steps.name: Boot rolls six
steps.title: The boot stops one square short of jail
steps.description: Six spaces up the red and yellow side, landing on Piccadilly with Go To Jail sitting immediately next to it.

footer.text: Roll a double and you go again — but a **third** double in one turn sends you to jail from wherever you are.

steps.name: Buys Park Lane
steps.title: The boot rolls eight and buys Park Lane
steps.description: Past Go To Jail, past the greens, onto the quieter of the two dark blues. £350, rent £35, and the beginning of something expensive.

steps.name: Hat rolls eight
steps.title: The hat crosses to Coventry Street
steps.description: Eight spaces past Free Parking and up the red side. Nothing happens on Coventry Street, which is the nicest thing about it.

steps.name: A two
steps.title: The boot rolls a two
steps.description: Park Lane, Super Tax, Mayfair. The shortest roll in the game and the only one that matters in this one.

data.note: a double — he rolls again afterwards

steps.name: Buys Mayfair
steps.title: The boot buys Mayfair for £400
steps.description: The most expensive square on the board, and the second dark blue. The set is complete, and unimproved rent doubles from £50 to £100 immediately.

steps.name: The bare site
steps.title: A deed, and nothing built on it
steps.description: Mayfair as bought costs £400 and charges £50. Owning Park Lane as well doubles that to £100 without a brick being laid.

footer.text: Unimproved rent **doubles** on a completed colour group. £50 → £100, for free.

steps.name: One house
steps.title: The first house — £200, and rent quadruples
steps.description: Houses cost £200 each here, and must go on evenly: one on Park Lane before a second goes on Mayfair. The first house is the best purchase in the game.

footer.text: The **even build rule**: no street in a set may be more than one house ahead of another.

steps.name: Two houses
steps.title: Two houses — £600
steps.description: Another £200 buys another £400 of rent. Park Lane goes to two at the same time, and is now charging £500.

steps.name: Three houses
steps.title: Three houses — £1,400
steps.description: The steepest rung on the ladder: £200 spent, £800 more rent. This is where most sets stop, because this is where the money runs out.

footer.text: Three houses is the value peak. Everything after this costs more than it returns per pound.

steps.name: Four houses
steps.title: Four houses — £1,700
steps.description: £200 for £300 more rent, the worst step on the card. It is bought for one reason: a hotel needs four houses under it, on both streets.

footer.text: Eight houses across the two streets: **£1,600** spent on building alone.

steps.name: The hotel
steps.title: The hotel — £200 and the four houses back
steps.description: A hotel does not sit on top of the houses; it replaces them. They return to the bank, where anyone else may buy them. Rent on Mayfair is now £2,000.

footer.text: Total outlay on Mayfair: **£400 + £1,000** in buildings. It repays itself on the first landing.

steps.name: Passing GO
steps.title: The boot rolls five and passes GO
steps.description: Off Mayfair, over the corner, and £200 lands in his hand for doing nothing but arriving. Then he stops on Income Tax.

footer.text: **£200** for passing GO — the same £200 whether you pass it or land on it exactly.

steps.name: In and straight out
steps.title: £200 in, £200 out
steps.description: The bank pays him for passing GO and takes it straight back for Income Tax. A whole lap of the board, net zero, and a hotel on Mayfair.

steps.name: Hat rolls ten
steps.title: The hat rolls ten onto Park Lane
steps.description: Ten spaces past the greens and the last Chance square, onto the first of the two dark blues. Four houses are standing on it.

steps.name: Rent: £1,100
steps.title: Park Lane with four houses — £1,100
steps.description: The same amber pipe as the £18 on Fleet Street, sixty-one times the size. He pays it, and has almost nothing left.

footer.text: Short of cash, you may mortgage, sell buildings back at **half price**, or trade. You may not simply decline to pay.

steps.name: Two again
steps.title: The hat rolls a two
steps.description: Park Lane, Super Tax, Mayfair. The same two spaces the boot rolled to buy it.

footer.text: Mayfair is one of the **least** landed-on squares on the board. It only has to happen once.

steps.name: Two thousand
steps.title: Mayfair, with a hotel — £2,000
steps.description: Rent is due the moment the token stops. The hat owns three streets, a station and £340; the bank will take the rest and there is still not enough.

footer.text: **£2,000.** Forty times the printed rent, and £1,982 more than the first rent of the game.
Everything he owns passes to the boot: deeds, cash, and the mortgaged ones at 10% interest to lift.

steps.name: Game over
steps.title: One player left
steps.description: A game ends when everyone but one is bankrupt. Two hours, one lap and a bit each, and the whole thing decided by a roll of two on the right square.

footer.text: Money that actually changed hands: about **£7,000**, and £3,100 of it was the last two landings.
The official rules have no auction pot, no Free Parking jackpot and no £400 for landing on GO. Every game you have played had house rules in it.
